title: Operating Systems
summary: How an operating system shares the CPU, memory, storage and devices between programs, and how it keeps them apart. Lectures cover the classic OS topics with Linux and Windows as examples, plus virtualisation and multicore hardware. Six individual C lab assignments on WebLab must be passed, and the grade comes from one closed-book exam.

basis.description: Slides of the CSE2430 lectures (10 lectures as text; Protection and Security only as the topic list in the final review), the CSE2430 lab assignments of 2024-25, and the 2023 and 2024 exam papers. Time shares count text slides; the security share is an estimate of one lecture.
basis.caveat: The material is from CSE2430, the older code, when the course was optional for students in the Systems variant and ran in quarter 3 of year 2. From 2026-27 the course is the compulsory core course CSE21C in year 2, quarter 1, so the schedule, the lab and the lecturers may differ. Cache Coherence and Windows shared one lecture slot, so their slide shares overstate their lecture time.

topics.name: OS structure and hardware support
know: The OS as resource manager and as a layer that hides hardware details, and the step from batch processing to multiprogramming to time sharing
Which hardware made each step possible: magnetic tape for batch work, a programmable timer for time sharing
Dual-mode execution: user mode versus kernel mode, the mode bit (MSR) and x86 protection rings
System calls, exceptions and interrupts: who raises each, and why each enters the kernel
How the mode bit changes when the kernel is entered and how a return-from-interrupt instruction switches back to user mode
Monolithic, modular and microkernel designs, and where device drivers live in each
do: Walk through a system call or an exception step by step, stating the processor mode at each step
Compare multiprogramming with time sharing, and argue for or against putting a driver inside the kernel
pitfalls: Mixing up exceptions (raised because the running code did something wrong) with interrupts (raised by a device to signal an event)
Saying when the mode bit is set but forgetting the switch back to user mode at the end of the handler

topics.name: Processes, IPC and CPU scheduling
know: From program to process: the ELF format, loading, the process control block and the states running, ready and blocked
fork, exec, wait and waitpid, exit, and the role of init as the first process
Signals, pipes and other IPC: shared memory, sockets, files
FIFO, SJF, SRT, priority and round-robin scheduling, and what each one optimises or sacrifices
Multilevel feedback queues and Linux niceness; why static priorities can starve jobs and how ageing fixes it
Real-time scheduling with rate-monotonic and earliest-deadline-first, and the CPU utilisation condition for meeting deadlines
Multiprocessor scheduling and the Linux schedulers up to CFS
do: Trace FIFO, SJF, SRT, priority and round-robin schedules for five processes and fill in each completion time
Draw an RMS or EDF schedule for three periodic tasks and spot a missed deadline
Count how many processes a fork loop creates, with or without waitpid
Say which state transitions are possible and what event causes each
pitfalls: Allowing blocked to running or ready to blocked: a blocked process always goes back through ready
In round-robin, letting a task keep the CPU after it finishes early instead of switching at once

topics.name: Threads, synchronisation and deadlock
know: Threads versus processes, the thread control block, and user-level, kernel-level and hybrid (N to M) threads with their trade-offs
POSIX threads and higher-level options: thread pools, OpenMP, Grand Central Dispatch
Race conditions, the Too Much Milk solutions, safety versus liveness, and Peterson's algorithm
Locks from disabling interrupts and from atomic instructions (test-and-set, compare-and-swap); spinlocks versus sleeping mutexes, ticket locks, the bakery algorithm and futexes
Condition variables, monitors (Mesa versus Hoare signalling) and semaphores, used on the producer-consumer queue
Priority inversion and its fixes, and Amdahl's law S(n) = 1 / ((1 - P) + P/n)
Deadlock: the four conditions, resource allocation graphs, prevention by lock ordering, avoidance with the Banker's algorithm, detection and recovery; deadlock versus livelock and starvation
do: Write pseudocode with semaphores or mutexes that forces an order between processes
Design a deadlock-free and starvation-free locking scheme for a dining philosophers variant
Build a semaphore out of a mutex and a sleep and wake-up mechanism
Choose between a spinlock and a kernel mutex for a given level of contention, and explain why
pitfalls: Checking a condition variable with if instead of a while loop
Assuming more threads always means more speed: Amdahl's law caps the speed-up

topics.name: Protection and security
know: The goals of protection, the least-privilege principle and the access matrix model with domains and owner and control rights
Ways to store the matrix: access lists, capability lists, lock and key
Threats: viruses, worms, ransomware, buffer overflows, port scanning, denial of service, and why humans are the weakest link (phishing, social engineering)
Buffer-overflow defences: a non-executable stack, stack canaries, compiler-inserted bounds checks
Authentication with passwords and one-way functions, symmetric keys, Diffie-Hellman key exchange, firewalls
do: Describe a realistic attack on a given system (session hijacking, replaying a car-key signal) and a practical defence against it
Explain how and why a program drops its own privileges in the access matrix model
pitfalls: Naming an attack without explaining why the proposed defence actually stops it, for example why a challenge-response defeats a replay

topics.name: Memory management and virtual memory
know: Heap allocation with first fit, best fit, worst fit and buddy allocation, and external versus internal fragmentation
Address spaces, relocation and translation; segmentation and its limits; paging
Page tables: simple forward-mapped, multi-level, hashed and inverted, plus the TLB
Page faults and how the MMU and the OS handle them together, and the effective access time formula with its simplifications
Page replacement: optimal, FIFO, LRU, clock and second-chance clock; local versus global replacement
Working sets, page-fault frequency, thrashing and swapping as load control
do: Work out where each malloc lands under first, best and worst fit after a series of allocations and frees
Fill a FIFO, LRU or clock replacement table for a request string and mark the page faults
Compute offset bits, the number of page table entries, the table size and the number of levels from the address and page sizes
Compute the effective memory access time from the access time, the clock speed, the disk transfer time and the fault rate
pitfalls: Counting page table entries from the physical address size instead of the virtual one
Ignoring the given access history (and, for clock, the starting hand position and reference bits) before the first request

topics.name: I/O and storage devices
know: Device access by polling, by interrupts and by DMA, and when each suits a device
Hard disk access time as seek time plus rotational delay plus transfer time, and disk capacity
Disk-head scheduling: FIFO, SSTF, SCAN, C-SCAN, LOOK and C-LOOK
RAID 0, 1, 3, 5 and 10: striping, mirroring and parity, with their read and write speeds
SSDs: the flash translation layer, garbage collection, write amplification, over-provisioning and wear
Buffered standard I/O versus Unix I/O, blocking versus non-blocking, and asynchronous APIs (POSIX aio, Linux aio, io_uring)
do: Order a list of track requests under four disk-scheduling algorithms and add up the tracks crossed
Compare the read or write time of an SSD with a RAID array of hard disks for a given file, with full calculations
Pick polling, interrupts or DMA for a described device and defend the choice
pitfalls: Turning SCAN or C-SCAN at the last request: in the model solutions they sweep to the disk edge, and C-SCAN counts the jump back
Using a full rotation instead of half a rotation as the average rotational delay

topics.name: File systems
know: Files, their attributes and operations; file descriptor table, open file table (with its reference count) and vnode table, and how fork shares open files
Directory structures, mounting, hard links versus soft links, and why hard links to directories are not allowed
Block allocation: contiguous, linked, FAT and indexed with the UNIX inode (direct, single, double and triple indirect blocks)
Free-space management with bitmaps and linked lists
Consistency: fsck, journaling in ext3, extents in ext4, and the ideas behind ReiserFS, XFS, ZFS and NTFS
do: Derive the maximum file size from the block size, address size and inode layout
Count the metadata blocks a file of a given size needs, including the inode and every indirect block
Explain how extents or journaling solve a stated problem
pitfalls: Forgetting the inode itself, or the extra indirect block under the doubly-indirect block, when counting metadata blocks

topics.name: Multicore and cache coherence
know: Shared-memory (UMA) and distributed shared-memory (NUMA) systems
Write-through versus write-back caches, and how private caches can hold stale copies
Snooping protocols and the MESI states modified, exclusive, shared and invalid
Coherence versus memory consistency, and weak consistency
Why spinning on a shared lock causes cache-line traffic, and the fix of spinning on the cached copy with plain loads before trying an atomic exchange
do: Trace the MESI state of a cache line through a sequence of reads and writes by two cores
Explain why a spinlock performs badly on many cores and how to reduce the traffic

topics.name: Windows internals
know: The path from MS-DOS to NT-based Windows and how NT's design differs from Unix
The layers: hardware abstraction layer, kernel, executive and its managers (object, I/O, virtual memory, security reference monitor)
Subsystems (Win32, WinRT/UWP, WSL) that translate their API calls into the native NT API
Threads as the unit of scheduling, priority boosts for the focused window, for threads woken from I/O and for servers handling a request
Stacked and filter drivers, the registry, NTFS recovery, and why the window manager runs in kernel mode
do: Name and explain two design differences between Windows NT and Unix
Explain a design choice (async tasks in UWP, kernel-mode window manager, filter drivers) with a concrete reason

topics.name: Virtualisation and containers
know: Why virtual machines are used, and the three goals safety, fidelity and performance
Type 1 and type 2 hypervisors, full emulation versus trap-and-emulate
Why some instruction sets cannot be virtualised by trap-and-emulate alone, and the fixes: binary translation, hardware assistance, para-virtualisation
Two-level address translation (nested or extended page tables) and I/O virtualisation
Containers versus virtual machines, with Docker and Kubernetes as examples
do: Explain why a program runs slower in a VM, and when it runs at almost native speed
Weigh para-virtualisation against pure virtualisation, and containers against VMs
pitfalls: Calling para-virtualisation a hardware feature: the guest is modified and knows it runs on a hypervisor

prerequisites: Programming in C: pointers, arrays, structs and bit operations (the lab starts with a C practice set)
Computer Organisation (CSE11C): registers, interrupts, caches and the memory hierarchy
Algorithms and Data Structures (CSE13C): queues, trees and linked lists
Comfort with powers of two and unit prefixes (KiB, MiB, GiB) without a calculator
Basic use of a Linux command line
practical: Six individual lab assignments in C on WebLab, all mandatory and pass/fail: processes and a small shell with fork and exec; multithreading with pthreads, niceness and parallel quicksort; concurrency with producer-consumer and semaphores; a buddy memory allocator; security, crafting a buffer-overflow payload and a loader that only runs correctly signed binaries; and a file system built with FUSE. All spec tests must pass, and a TA signs off each one by checking that you understand your code. The lab does not count towards the grade, but failing it gives a 1.
studyAdvice: Memory, scheduling and I/O together carry almost half of the exam points; give them most of your revision time.

Drill the fixed calculation exercises until they are routine: scheduling tables, page replacement tables, disk-head scheduling, heap fits, page table sizes and inode metadata blocks. They are about a third of every paper.
Windows takes 12 percent of the slides and about 6 percent of the points. Learn a short list of facts (subsystems, priority boosts, filter drivers, NT versus Unix) rather than the whole history.
Multicore and cache coherence earned no points on the 2023 and 2024 papers. Study it last, but keep the spinlock and futex part, which is examined under synchronisation.
The security slides are not in the archive. Work from the topic list in the final review and the Homework 5 solutions, and practise describing an attack together with its defence.
Do the homework sets after each lecture and check them against the solutions in the archive (Homework 1 to 5 and 8): they are written in the exam style.
Keep a week ahead in the lab, as the course advises, so you can ask questions before the sign-off; the shell, threading and concurrency work also helps on the exam questions about those topics.
